newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: UN okays some Iraq spare parts,defers other issues.
newsitem.headline: UN okays some Iraq spare parts,defers other issues.

text.p: The United Nations sanctions committee on Iraq approved Thursday the importation of some spare parts for one of Iraq's pipelines, but again deferred broader questions to a later date.

Separately, a total of $149 million from the proceeds of Iraqi oil sales had been paid as of Thursday into the U.N. escrow account at the New York Branch of the Banque Nationale de Paris, a U.N. source said.
Of the total amount, $53.1 million had so far been paid out, including $33.9 million to the U.N. Gulf War reparations fund and the remainder for various other U.N. costs, the source said.
On the question of allowing Iraq to raise the current cap on oil exports of $2 billion under the "oil-for-food" plan, diplomats said the issue has not yet come up for discussion.
Iraqi officials have said frequently that Baghdad will look for the ceiling to be raised when the agreement is reviewed. But diplomats said no official request has been submitted to the U.N.
"It depends on whether we see a need. But it is really too early to tell," a western diplomat on the sanctions committee said.

The oil deal, which allows Iraq to use about two-thirds of the proceeds to pay for food and other humanitarian items under strict U.N. supervision, came into effect on December 10 and comes up for a 90-day review in early March.
However, any revisions to its terms are not expected to be considered until the agreement comes up for renewal after 180 days, the diplomat said.

The sanctions committee on Thursday approved a request made in October by Turkey for basic equipment needed to repair immediate defects on the Kirkuk-Yumurtalik pipeline, which carries the majority of Iraq's oil under the terms of the oil deal.

However, a decision on a second list of parts submitted by Turkey in November for medium- and long-term repairs to the pipeline was deferred, according to Portuguese ambassador Antonio Monteiro, current chairman of the sanctions committee.

The committee also deferred for later decision Turkey's request, made last August before implementation of the deal, for a lifting of its imports of Iraqi oil and oil products because of urgent economic need.
Diplomats said that decision was less pressing, as Turkey was a major buyer of Iraqi oil since implementation and was benefitting from fees paid for use of the pipeline.
The committee did not discuss any new oil contracts at Thursday's meeting. So far, 26 contracts have been approved and there are none pending, according to U.N. officials.

There had been some concern that the total value of the contracts would exceed the $1 billion allowed over the first 90 days -- which led to some contracts being cut back. However, that concern has waned as oil prices have fallen, diplomats said.
